newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Letter bomb found at U.N. addressed to Arabic paper.
newsitem.headline: Letter bomb found at U.N. addressed to Arabic paper.

text.p: A letter bomb addressed to the U.N. bureau of the Arabic-language newspaper Al-Hayat was found in a messenger room on Monday at U.N. headquarters in New York, a U.N. spokesman said.
A second suspicious envelope was being examined, he said.
Security guards evacuated and closed off parts of the press area at the U.N. complex and the New York police bomb squad was called in.
Earlier, a letter bomb exploded at the London office of Al-Hayat, a Saudi Arabian-owned newspaper, wounding two security guards. Four more suspect devices were found there later, British police said.

U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said the bomb sent to the United Nations was in a greeting-card sized envelope addressed to Al-Hayat -- similar to several devices mailed earlier this month to the same newspaper's Washington bureau.
"It is a live bomb and it is going to be exploded (under controlled conditions) in the basement," he said.
The bomb had not been detected in the basement area where mail is first sorted but after it reached a messenger station on the second floor, Eckhard said.

A U.N. source said mail delivered to the United Nations was normally scanned as a security precaution. The precautions were stepped up after Al-Hayat's U.N. correspondent, Raghida Dergham, informed U.N. security of the London incident.

The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation launched an international investigation earlier this month after eight letter bombs made to look like Christmas cards were mailed from Egypt to the United States.

Four arrived at Al-Hayat's Washington office and a fifth was found in the mail system. Three other devices turned up in the area around Leavenworth federal prison in Kansas. None of the potentially lethal devices exploded.

Mohammad Salameh, a militant Moslem jailed for life for the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, is in Leavenworth, as are Victor Alvarez and Mohammed Saleh who were convicted of plotting to blow up U.N. headquarters and other New York targets.
The FBI has dismissed as speculative reports it is investigating a possible connection between the letter bombs and these cases.
